analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses in employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights contracts.
analysis.headline: Despite 26 Senate cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have voided contract clauses that force workers and consumers to settle disputes in private arbitration instead of court. Companies write these clauses into employment paperwork and the fine print of consumer contracts, and they take effect before any dispute exists, so the person signing usually has no real choice. Under the bill, claims about wages, discrimination, consumer fraud, antitrust, and civil rights could go to a judge and jury, and only arbitration agreed to after a dispute arises would still count.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with discrimination or wage claims, consumers cheated by a company, and people with antitrust or civil rights claims would regain the right to take their cases to a public court, and to band together in class actions instead of being pushed one at a time into a private, confidential arbitration process chosen by the company. The bill's own findings state that most consumers and employees have little or no meaningful choice whether to accept arbitration and are often unaware they gave up their rights [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers forced into arbitration

how_it_helps.text: It makes predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, so those cases can be heard in court [S2][S3].

It restores access to class actions: the antitrust provision specifically covers disputes where plaintiffs seek class certification, and consumer and civil rights claims would again be heard together in public rather than funneled into individual private arbitration [S3].
It puts a judge, not the arbitrator the company selected, in charge of deciding whether an arbitration agreement applies, and applies federal law in making that call [S2][S3].

It preserves arbitration that is genuinely voluntary: the bill's findings state arbitration is acceptable when consent is truly voluntary and occurs after a dispute arises, and it leaves collective bargaining agreements between employers and unions in place [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and sellers of consumer products, credit, and securities would pay: they could no longer use fine-print arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court, so they would face public lawsuits, jury trials, and class actions, with the litigation costs and damages that come with them. Companies argue that means slower, costlier dispute resolution and larger, less predictable losses; supporters reply that is the price of a public court system that sets precedent others can rely on [S3].

drawbacks.text: Court litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for both sides, and some workers and consumers with small claims might find a lawsuit harder to pursue than a single arbitration hearing; the bill would push more disputes into that slower system [S3].

Class actions deliver uneven results: class members often receive small individual payments while plaintiffs' lawyers collect large fees, so restoring class access benefits those members less than the headline suggests.
The bill takes effect for any dispute arising on or after enactment, so companies would face immediate uncertainty about which pending contract terms remain enforceable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large for the people covered: the right to have a discrimination, fraud, or antitrust claim heard in a public court, with a judge, a jury, appeal, and precedent. The costs are the higher litigation expenses companies would bear and the uneven value of class actions for individual class members. The strongest honest objection is that not every arbitration is worse for the claimant — but the bill's design addresses that by leaving arbitration fully available when it is agreed to after a dispute arises, which is when a person actually has a choice [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Al Franken introduced the Arbitration Fairness Act of 2017 in the Senate on March 7, 2017, with 23 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary — the only action it ever received [S5].

The cosponsor list grew to 26 senators (25 Democrats and 1 Independent), but the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that put forced arbitration clauses in employment and consumer contracts — banks, large employers, and others — are better off, because they kept the ability to push disputes into private arbitration and block class actions. Workers and consumers are no worse off than before, but gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms that use forced arbitration clauses

for.name: Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up cosponsors

for.name: 1 Senate Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing the total to 26

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee from introduction until the Congress ended

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed limits on mandatory arbitration clauses, which its member companies rely on to keep disputes out of court

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Judiciary chair, the bill never moved — no Republican cosponsored it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to require workers to sign away the right to sue over discrimination, harassment, and wage claims as a condition of a job, forcing those disputes into open court. Their interest in keeping the clauses runs directly against workers' access to court.

Arbitration clauses in credit card, loan, and account agreements block customers from banding together in class actions over fees and fraud; the bill would void them for consumer disputes, exposing the industry to class litigation it currently avoids [S3].

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care providers
industries.note: Admission paperwork commonly requires families to arbitrate any negligence or abuse claim; the bill's civil rights and consumer provisions would take those cases back to court, where outcomes and standards are public.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers (AAA, JAMS and private arbitrators)
industries.note: Their business depends on mandatory arbitration clauses routing employment and consumer disputes to paid private forums; the bill would shrink that market to disputes voluntarily submitted after they arise.
